items: 1 cup besan (gram flour / chickpea flour), sieved
1 cup ghee, plus ¼ cup neutral oil
groups.title: For the besan mixture

kidVersion.text: Mysore pak is already vegetarian and nut-free. For young cooks: let an adult handle the hot sugar syrup and the pouring — kids can grease the tray, sieve the besan, and press the cardamom. Cut into small bite-size squares; the rich ghee means a little goes a long way.
kidVersion.title: Kid-friendly version

method: Grease a tray or plate generously with ghee and keep it ready — the mixture sets fast.
In a heavy pan, dissolve the sugar in the water and boil to one-string consistency: a drop pressed between thumb and finger pulls a single thread.
Lower the flame and add the sieved besan a spoonful at a time, stirring constantly so no lumps form.
Heat the ghee and oil together until very hot. Pour a ladleful into the besan mixture and stir; it will froth and bubble. Keep stirring until the fat is absorbed, then repeat 4–5 times.
When the mixture turns pale gold, smells nutty, and leaves the sides of the pan, pour it into the greased tray immediately. Level gently.
After 5 minutes, cut into squares while still warm. Let cool fully (about 30 minutes) before separating. Store airtight.
recipes.name: Mysore Pak
recipes.seasonWhy: Diwali season (Nov 6–10): ghee-rich sweets are made for Lakshmi puja prasad and gifting.
recipes.story: In 1935, Kakasura Madappa, the chief cook of the Mysore Palace, was asked by King Krishna Raja Wadiyar IV for a new sweet. With gram flour, ghee and sugar on hand, he improvised — and the melt-in-the-mouth fudge that emerged was named “Mysuru paka,” a sweet from Mysore. It remains the Diwali sweet of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.

items: ½ cup fresh coriander (cilantro) leaves, chopped
¾ tsp salt, or to taste
groups.title: For the guacamole

items: Tortilla chips or warm corn tortillas
groups.title: To serve

kidVersion.text: Skip the jalapeño entirely for a mild version kids love — the lime and creamy avocado carry it. Let kids do the mashing (great fork practice) and the lime squeezing with a grown-up nearby.
kidVersion.title: Kid-friendly version

method: Halve the avocados, remove the pits, and scoop the flesh into a bowl.
Mash with a fork until creamy but still a little chunky — texture is the point.
Fold in the onion, jalapeño, coriander, and lime juice. Season with salt.
Taste and adjust: more lime for brightness, more chili for heat.
Serve immediately with tortilla chips. To hold briefly, press plastic wrap directly onto the surface to slow browning.
recipes.name: Guacamole
recipes.seasonWhy: Summer: avocados are at their creamy peak and the fresh version needs no cooking.
recipes.story: From the Nahuatl “ahuacamolli” — avocado sauce — guacamole has been pounded in volcanic-stone molcajetes since Aztec times. It is laid on Día de los Muertos ofrendas (Nov 1–2) among the favorite foods of returning souls, and eaten by the living with equal ceremony.

kidVersion.text: Caffeine-free “chai” for kids: swap the black tea for rooibos leaves (same dark color, no caffeine), keep the spices and milk, and go light on the sugar. Always let an adult handle the boiling and pouring.
kidVersion.title: Kid-friendly version

method: Crush the cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, and ginger coarsely with a mortar and pestle.
Bring the water to a rolling boil, add the crushed spices, and simmer 2–3 minutes until fragrant.
Add the tea leaves and boil 1 minute more for strength.
Pour in the milk and sugar; bring back to a boil, then simmer 2 minutes until the color turns a rich caramel brown.
Strain into cups and serve piping hot.
recipes.name: Masala Chai
recipes.seasonWhy: Winter: warming spices for cold mornings; chai stalls do their best business in the cool months.
recipes.story: Tea arrived in India on British plantations, but Indians made the bitter colonial brew their own — simmered with milk, sugar, and the spice box: ginger (adrak), cardamom (elaichi), cloves. The half-glass “cutting chai” of Mumbai's trains and street corners turned it into the country's everyday ritual.
